meta.title: Quadratic Equations
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 4 (jemh104.pdf, printed pages 38–48)

board_asks: solving by factorisation & the quadratic formula, the discriminant (nature of roots), and word problems — these carry almost every mark here.

big_idea.body: A quadratic equation is any equation you can write as $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where $a \neq 0$. The whole chapter answers one question: what values of $x$ make this true? Those values are the roots. You'll learn to find them (factorisation, the quadratic formula), decide whether they exist (the discriminant), relate them to the coefficients, and turn real situations into equations you can solve.

definitions.verbatim: A quadratic equation in the variable x is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers, a ≠ 0.
definitions.plain: any equation that simplifies to degree 2. If the $x^2$ term survives simplification, it is quadratic — always simplify FIRST before deciding (NCERT's Example 2 warning).

definitions.verbatim: In general, a real number α is called a root of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0 if aα² + bα + c = 0. We also say that x = α is a solution of the quadratic equation, or that α satisfies the quadratic equation.
definitions.plain: a value of $x$ that makes the equation true — plug it in and the LHS becomes $0$. Same thing as a zero of the polynomial $ax^2+bx+c$.

definitions.verbatim: Since b² – 4ac determines whether the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 has real roots or not, b² – 4ac is called the discriminant of this quadratic equation.
definitions.plain: $D = b^2 - 4ac$. When a question asks about the NATURE of roots (or “find $k$”), compute $D$ first — its sign answers the question without solving for $x$.

definitions.verbatim: So, a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 has (i) two distinct real roots, if b² – 4ac > 0, (ii) two equal real roots, if b² – 4ac = 0, (iii) no real roots, if b² – 4ac < 0.
definitions.plain: $D>0$: cuts the x-axis twice · $D=0$: just touches it · $D<0$: never meets it. In answers, always say “no real roots”, not “no roots”.

definitions.verbatim: Quadratic formula: The roots of a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are given by (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, provided b² – 4ac ≥ 0.
definitions.plain: $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$ — the fallback that always works when $b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$, e.g. when the middle term won't split.

source.note: Summary point 4; the printed stacked fraction is linearised with brackets

definitions.verbatim: That is, ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0 is called the standard form of a quadratic equation.
Note that the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c and the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are the same.
You have observed, in Chapter 2, that a quadratic polynomial can have at most two zeroes. So, any quadratic equation can have atmost two roots.

source.note: “atmost” is NCERT's own spelling in the second sentence — preserved verbatim

definitions.verbatim: If we can factorise ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0, into a product of two linear factors, then the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 can be found by equating each factor to zero.

concepts.title: Solving by factorisation
concepts.body: Split the middle term so the product of the two parts equals $a \cdot c$, factor by grouping into two linear factors, then equate each factor to zero — the roots fall out.

concepts.title: The quadratic formula
concepts.body: $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$, valid when $b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$. The fallback when factorisation is hard — write $a$, $b$, $c$ with their signs before substituting.

concepts.title: Nature of roots via the discriminant
concepts.body: $D = b^2 - 4ac$. $D>0$ → two distinct real roots · $D=0$ → two equal real roots · $D<0$ → no real roots. The graph shows it best:
concepts.tested: “find k” for equal roots — up to 5 marks (CBSE 2024, 30/5/1 Q32a)

concepts.title: Roots & coefficients (sum & product)
concepts.body: For roots $\alpha, \beta$: $\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta = \dfrac{c}{a}$. Build an equation from given roots: $x^2 - (\alpha+\beta)x + \alpha\beta = 0$. ⚑ Syllabus note: catalogued under Polynomials (quadratic zeroes–coefficient relationship) — applied here.

concepts.title: Word problems → equation
concepts.body: Translate the situation (area, ages, speed, consecutive numbers) into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, solve, and REJECT the root the situation forbids — a negative length or age, or an excluded value like $k \neq -1$.
concepts.tested: Long applied problem — a fixture of Sections C/D

examples.problem_verbatim: Find the roots of the quadratic equation 6x² – x – 2 = 0.

solution_steps.text: $6x^2 - x - 2 = 6x^2 + 3x - 4x - 2$ — the two parts multiply to $6x^2 \times (-2)…$ i.e. product $-12x^2$, sum $-x$.
The roots of $6x^2 - x - 2 = 0$ are the values of $x$ for which $(3x - 2)(2x + 1) = 0$: so $3x - 2 = 0$ or $2x + 1 = 0$.
$x = \dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. NCERT then verifies both satisfy the equation.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the split, 1 for the factorisation, 1 for BOTH roots. Writing only one root is the classic lost mark — NCERT itself verifies both.

examples.problem_verbatim: Find the discriminant of the quadratic equation 2x² – 4x + 3 = 0, and hence find the nature of its roots.

solution_steps.text: The equation is of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with $a = 2$, $b = -4$, $c = 3$.
$D < 0$ → the given equation has no real roots.
solution_steps.concept_tag: nature from the sign of D

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape: 1 for computing $D$ with correct signs — $(-4)^2 = +16$ — and 1 for the conclusion stated in words (“no real roots”).

examples.shape: Equal roots — find them · NCERT Example 9
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the discriminant of the equation 3x² – 2x + 1/3 = 0 and hence find the nature of its roots. Find them, if they are real.

solution_steps.text: $D = 0$ → the equation has two equal real roots.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for $D$ computed, 1 for “two equal real roots”, 1 for actually finding them via $-b/2a$ — the “find them, if they are real” half is where the last mark sits.

examples.shape: Word problem · NCERT Example 8 (pole on a circular park)
examples.problem_verbatim: A pole has to be erected at a point on the boundary of a circular park of diameter 13 metres in such a way that the differences of its distances from two diametrically opposite fixed gates A and B on the boundary is 7 metres. Is it possible to do so? If yes, at what distances from the two gates should the pole be erected?

solution_steps.text: Let $P$ be the pole with $BP = x$ m; the difference of distances is 7 m, so $AP = (x + 7)$ m. $AB = 13$ m is a diameter, so $\angle APB = 90°$.

solution_steps.lead: Is it possible? Ask the discriminant.
solution_steps.text: $b^2 - 4ac = 7^2 - 4 \times 1 \times (-60) = 289 > 0$ → two real roots, so the pole CAN be erected.
$x$ is a distance, so it must be positive — ignore $-12$. The pole goes 5 m from gate B and 12 m from gate A.

examples.mark_logic: Case/competency shape (4–5 marks): modelling + the equation (1–2) · discriminant feasibility check (1) · solving (1) · rejecting the negative root and stating BOTH distances (1).

source.note: problem on p.45, solution runs to p.46

examples.shape: “Find k” for equal roots · CBSE 2024 board paper
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the value of 'k' for which the quadratic equation (k + 1)x² – 6(k + 1)x + 3(k + 9) = 0, k ≠ – 1 has real and equal roots.

solution_steps.text: The paper itself excludes $k = -1$ (it would kill the $x^2$ term). Reject it: $k = 3$.

examples.mark_logic: Board mark scheme (Section D, 5 marks): $D = 0$ stated (1) · substitution (1) · simplification to $k^2 - 2k - 3 = 0$ (1) · solving (1) · rejecting $k = -1$ and concluding $k = 3$ (1). Miss the rejection and you lose the final mark.

strategies.text: Go straight to $D = b^2 - 4ac$. Don't solve for $x$.
Factorise first; if the middle term won't split, use the formula.
Name $x$ → build the equation → standard form → solve → reject the impossible root.
Check $a \neq 0$ — an excluded value in the question is a mark waiting to be lost.

pitfalls.text: Forgetting to reject the invalid root — negative length / age / count, or an excluded value like $k \neq -1$.
Sign slips in $D$ — when $b$ is negative, $(-4)^2 = +16$, not $-16$.
Sign error in form-the-equation — the middle term is $-(\alpha+\beta)$, not $+$.

third_tab_content.name: The quadratic formula — where it comes from
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT's history box (p.39) credits Sridharacharya (C.E. 1025) with the quadratic formula, derived “by the method of completing the square”. In the 2026-27 syllabus, completing the square is NOT an assessed solution method — you solve by factorisation or the formula. Use this derivation to understand where the formula and the $b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$ condition come from, not as an exam technique.

steps.claim: Divide through by $a$ — allowed precisely because $a \neq 0$.
Complete the square: add $\left(\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2$ to both sides.
The left side is now a perfect square.

steps.justification: Real only when $b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$ — this is exactly where the discriminant condition comes from.

source.note: historical attribution only — the rationalised 2026-27 chapter no longer prints this derivation; the formula itself is Summary point 4, p.47
